clips.title: AI Coding Agents Are Reward Hacking: 1,300 Runs, 132 Bypasses
clips.why: A short tour of real reward hacks by coding agents, from the research by METR and OpenAI.
look: What a reward hack looks like in practice: the agent passes the check instead of solving the task.
How often the hack goes through the tests themselves or the code that runs them.
clips.after: Locked checks take the judge out of the agent's reach, so the cheap path is closed and only the real fix turns CI green.

clips.title: TDD Reward Hacking: Why Your Coding Agent is Cheating
clips.why: He shows tests that still pass but prove less: weak assertions and missing checks, the kind of change weakened-tests looks for.
look: What a weak assertion looks like next to a strong one.
Why a passing test that checks less is worse than a failing one: nobody looks at it again.
How mutation testing catches what a diff check cannot.
clips.after: Our weakened-tests check catches the visible signs in the diff; mutation testing is the slower, deeper check that later lessons add at night.

clips.title: Dana Baril - Eliminating Alert Fatigue: Reducing False Positives Through Better Engineering
clips.why: A security engineer from Tel Aviv on why alerts that are often wrong end up ignored, and what that costs.
look: What alert fatigue does to the people who receive the alerts.
Why reducing false positives is engineering work, not a matter of telling people to pay attention.
clips.after: That is why weakened-tests is calibrated on fifty merged pull requests before it is switched on: at most one false alarm in ten.

clips.title: Pyproject.toml: The modern Python project definition file, explained
clips.why: If you have never opened a pyproject.toml, this shows what lives in it, so the partial lock makes sense.
look: Where the dependencies are listed, the part the upgrade fixer must be able to change.
That the same file holds sections for other tools, which is where coverage and lint settings live.
clips.after: locked-checks leaves [project] open for the upgrade fixer and locks the [tool.*] sections that judge it.

practice.q: An agent's pull request changes frontend/src/App.tsx and frontend/vitest.config.js. A person's pull request changes the same two files. What does locked-checks say?

options.why: Human pull requests pass straight through; the reviewer sees the change.

options.text: The agent's fails and lists frontend/vitest.config.js; the person's passes.
options.why: The test runner's config judges the agent, so only agents are blocked from it.

options.text: Both pass, because App.tsx is not locked.
options.why: One locked file is enough to fail an agent's pull request.

practice.q: Finish the comparison so key order and formatting do not count as a change.
practice.why: It compares parsed values key by key in any order. JSON.stringify would see moved keys as a change.

practice.q: Put the work of switching on weakened-tests in order.
items: Write the patterns for skips, removed assertions and thresholds
Run them over the last fifty merged fcp pull requests
Count the false alarms per pattern
Narrow or drop any pattern with more than one false alarm in ten pull requests
Switch the check on for every pull request, as warnings
practice.why: A flag earns its place by being right most of the time; calibration comes before anyone sees it.

practice.q: Why does locked-checks pass a person's pull request that edits .github/workflows/frontend-ci.yaml?

options.text: Because people never make mistakes in CI files.
options.why: They do, which is why a person reviews every pull request.

options.text: Because the check is about agents changing their own judge; people change CI for good reasons and the reviewer sees it.
options.why: The wall is for the case where the one being judged edits the judge.

options.text: Because workflow files are protected by GitHub anyway.
options.why: Only the App lacks the workflows permission. People with write access can change them.
